chunks: "Positive. An inductor's impedance is j omega L , so its reactance is plus omega L .
A capacitor's impedance is 1 over (j omega C) , which is -j over ( omega C) , so its reactance is negative.
The sign comes straight from the math: the inductor's voltage is proportional to the derivative of current, and differentiating a sinusoid multiplies by plus j omega .
Physically, positive reactance means the voltage leads the current by 90 degrees, or the current lags.
The mnemonic I use is 'ELI the ICE man': in an inductor, L, the voltage E comes before the current I. The sign is useful because it tells you which way a circuit leans.
If I put an inductor and a capacitor in series, I just add the reactances. Below resonance the capacitor's negative reactance is bigger, so the combination looks capacitive.
Above resonance the inductor wins and it looks inductive. At resonance they cancel to zero, which is the whole idea behind impedance matching and LC tanks.
One caveat on real parts: a real inductor only has positive reactance up to its self-resonant frequency.
Above that, the winding capacitance dominates and the reactance goes negative, so it actually behaves like a capacitor."
